prompt: A coworker drops to the break-room floor, unresponsive, with no normal breathing. You start chest compressions. How deep should each push go?

options.text: At least 2 inches, no deeper than 2.4 inches
About 1 inch, so a cracked rib is less likely
About 3 inches, so the push is clearly forceful
Just until the chest wall barely begins to move

explanation: Adult compressions are at least 2 inches (5 cm) and no deeper than 2.4 inches (6 cm). That range moves blood. Shallower pushes do not fill the arteries, and going past 2.4 inches raises the chance of chest injury. Press on the center of the chest.

distractorExplanations.b: One inch is too shallow for an adult. The floor is 2 inches, not a lighter push chosen to protect the ribs.
distractorExplanations.c: Three inches is past the 2.4-inch maximum. Extra depth raises the chance of breaking ribs or injuring organs under the breastbone.
distractorExplanations.d: A push that only starts the chest moving is too shallow. Adult depth is a measured 2 to 2.4 inches, not a token press.

prompt: You are compressing the chest of an unresponsive adult who is not breathing. A bystander asks how fast your hands should press. What rate do you keep?

options.text: 60 to 80 compressions in each minute
100 to 120 compressions in each minute
140 to 160 compressions in each minute
180 to 200 compressions in each minute

explanation: The adult compression rate is 100 to 120 per minute. Slower than that does not move enough blood to the brain. Faster than that keeps the chest from recoiling, so each push gets shallower even if you are working harder.

distractorExplanations.c: One hundred forty to 160 is above the range. Hands that fast usually bounce and skip the recoil the heart needs.
distractorExplanations.d: One hundred eighty to 200 is about twice a useful rate and produces shallow compressions that move little blood.

prompt: During CPR on an adult in a hallway, you leave your weight on the chest after each push. What should you change?

options.text: Lean harder so the next compression starts deeper
Stop for several seconds so your arms can rest
Let the chest rise fully before the next push
Speed up and skip the release to raise the rate

explanation: Full chest recoil lets the heart refill with blood between compressions. Weight left on the chest blocks that refill, so the next push moves less blood. Release the pressure and let the chest come all the way up without taking your hands off the spot.

distractorExplanations.a: Pressing harder while you keep leaning does not fix recoil. Weight left on the chest is what stops the heart from filling.
distractorExplanations.b: A rest of several seconds is a long pause with no circulation. Recoil is a quick release between pushes, not a break in CPR.
distractorExplanations.d: Skipping the release to go faster removes the refill. Keep 100 to 120 per minute and let the chest rise each time.
